questions.question: State the five questions used to judge whether a food suits a refugee camp, and apply them to fresh milk, milk powder, bread and maize meal.
questions.expected_answer: Does it keep at room temperature in a tent and for how long; is it nutritious and which food group is it; does it travel light and compact for the nourishment it carries and survive rough handling; can it be cooked in a big pot by tired people with little fuel, water and time; and will these people eat it, considering religion, culture, babies and the elderly. Fresh milk is nutritious, needs no cooking and is accepted, but sours in a day without a fridge and is heavy, so it fails. Milk powder keeps a year sealed, weighs a tenth as much, is mixed with boiled water and is accepted, so it passes. Bread keeps about three days, is bulky, needs no cooking and is popular, so it is useful only for the first days. Maize meal keeps months in a dry sack, is light and energy dense, cooks in twenty minutes as pap with water and a fire, and is the staple of most South Africans, so it passes every question and leads every food parcel.

questions.question: Describe the main food processing methods that make foods suitable for an emergency camp, with examples, including fortification, and state the costs of processing.
questions.expected_answer: Drying removes the water that bacteria and moulds need, so dried beans, lentils, rice, dried fruit, biltong and milk powder keep for months and weigh far less than fresh. Milling grinds grain into meal or flour that cooks quickly, maize meal in twenty minutes against hours for whole kernels, saving fuel. Tinning seals cooked food in cans heated to kill all organisms, so pilchards, beans, tomatoes and corned meat keep for years and need no cooking, at the cost of the weight of can and liquid. Fermenting preserves and flavours, as in amasi, mageu and bread. Salting and smoking preserve fish and meat. Fortifying adds nutrients at the mill, and South African maize meal and wheat flour must by law contain added vitamin A, iron, zinc and B vitamins, which matters where vegetables are scarce. Sealed, measured packaging protects against damp, rats and dirt. The costs are loss of some vitamins and fibre, added weight, salt or sugar, and the energy and factories processing needs, so processed foods are mixed with fresh local onions, cabbage and potatoes.

questions.question: Give a suitable list of foods for a refugee camp arranged by food group, and explain how it is adjusted for the mix of people and for the camp kitchen's fuel.
questions.expected_answer: Staples: fortified maize meal first, rice, samp, wheat flour or bread for the first days, potatoes. Proteins: dried beans and lentils, tinned pilchards and tinned beans, soya mince, eggs if available locally, milk powder, peanut butter. Fats: sunflower oil, peanut butter, margarine. Vegetables and fruit: tinned tomatoes, onions, cabbage, pumpkin or butternut, dried fruit and oranges in season; plus salt, sugar, tea and spices for acceptability and morale. For babies over six months, soft maize porridge with milk powder and mashed butternut; for toddlers and the elderly, softer, smaller, more frequent meals enriched with oil and peanut butter; for the sick, oral rehydration solution then soft food; for pregnant and breastfeeding women, extra protein; for Muslim families, pilchards and beans rather than pork; for families from elsewhere, rice as an alternative staple. For fuel, beans need soaking and an hour's cooking so a bean day alternates with a no-cook pilchard day, pap with pilchard and tomato relish takes twenty minutes in one pot per fifty, and lentil, onion and cabbage soup is one pot of soft food for all.
